# Data Loading 

First, we must load our data to get a sense of what information we will be looking at! 

```{r}
#saving my input data file 
fna.data <- "WisconsinCancer.csv"

wisc.df <- read.csv(fna.data, row.names = 1)

head(wisc.df, 4)

```

Now, we should separate the diagnosis from the measurements

```{r}
wisc.data <- wisc.df[,-1]

diagnosis <- as.factor(wisc.df$diagnosis)
```

# Exploratory Data Analysis: 

```{r}
dim(wisc.df)
colnames(wisc.df)
head(wisc.df)
```

>Q1.How many observations are in this dataset? 

```{r}
nrow(wisc.data)
```

>Q2. How many of the observations have a malignant diagnosis?

```{r}
table(diagnosis)

```

>Q3. How many variables/features in the data are suffixed with _mean?

```{r}
length(grep("_mean$", colnames(wisc.data)))
```

# Principal Component Analysis: 

First, check if the data needs to be scaled before we actually perform the PCA! 

```{r}
colMeans(wisc.data)

apply(wisc.data,2,sd)
```

### Performing PCA 

Now, perform the PCA

```{r}
wisc.pr <- prcomp(wisc.data, scale. = TRUE)
summary(wisc.pr)
```

>Q4. From your results, what proportion of the original variance is captured by the first principal component (PC1)?

From my results above, PC1 was able to capture 44.27% of the original variable in the dataset. 

>Q5. How many principal components (PCs) are required to describe at least 70% of the original variance in the data?

3 PCs are required to explain at least 70% of the original variance as they explain around 72.64%! 

>Q6. How many principal components (PCs) are required to describe at least 90% of the original variance in the data?

To describe at least 90% of the original variance, 7 Pcs are required as they explain around 91.01%!


### Interpreting PCA Results 

Create a biplot to visualize the PCA Results!

```{r}
biplot(wisc.pr)
```

>Q7. What stands out to you about this plot? Is it easy or difficult to understand? Why?

Based on the results of the plot, it is really difficult for me to interepret. While there is an attempt of the plot trying to show a relationship with two different colors, there are just so many variables that are hard to decipher. Also, there is a lot of crowding in the plot which makes it hard to understand the patterns and what we are trying to look for! 

Now, let's generate a scatter plot of each observation along PCs 1 and 2: 

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(as.data.frame(wisc.pr$x)) + aes(PC1, PC2, col = diagnosis) + geom_point()

```

>Q8. Generate a similar plot for principal components 1 and 3. What do you notice about these plots? 

```{r}
ggplot(as.data.frame(wisc.pr$x)) + aes(PC1, PC3, col = diagnosis) + geom_point()
```

The main change we made in these two plots was to PC3! Because of this, both plots still similarly showed a comparison(difference) in the malignant vs benign samples! Malignant is mainly grouped onto left while benign was mainly grouped towards the right. However, towards the middle is where we see some overlap. For the PC1 vs PC2 plot, the separation is clearer than that of PC1 and PC3. In the second one, there is a larger overlap of the points which helps us realize that PC1 plays a huge role in the differences between the two samples! 

### Variance Explained 

First, we calculate the variance of each principle value

```{r}
pr.var <- wisc.pr$sdev^2
head(pr.var)
```

Then, calculate the variance explained by each priniciple and create a plot! 

```{r}
pve <- pr.var / sum(pr.var)

plot(c(1,pve), xlab = "Principal Component", 
     ylab = "Proportion of Variance Explained", 
     ylim = c(0, 1), type = "o")
```
An Alternative scree plot for the same data can also be created! 

```{r} 
barplot(pve, ylab = "Percent of Variance Explained",
     names.arg=paste0("PC",1:length(pve)), las=2, axes = FALSE)
axis(2, at=pve, labels=round(pve,2)*100 )
```

### Communicating PCA Results 

>Q9.  For the first principal component, what is the component of the loading vector (i.e. wisc.pr$rotation[,1]) for the feature concave.points_mean? This tells us how much this original feature contributes to the first PC. Are there any features with larger contributions than this one?

First, we find the loading value for concave.points_mean

```{r}
wisc.pr$rotation["concave.points_mean", 1]
```

Based on the results, the component of PC1 loading vector that corresponds to that specific function was around -0.26085. This means that this feature has the largest absolute loading and has a strong contribution to PC1! 


# Hierarchical Clustering 

Here, we want to do hierarchical clustering with our OG data to see if there are any grouping patterns of the malignant and benign clusters! 

First, we will scale the data and assign it: 

```{r}
data.scaled <- scale(wisc.data)
```

Next, calculate the distances between all pairs of observations: 

```{r}
data.dist <- dist(data.scaled)
```

Finally, create a hierarchical clustering model: 

```{r}
wisc.hclust <- hclust(data.dist, method = "complete")
wisc.hclust
```

# Results of Hierarchical Clustering 

>Q10. Using the plot() and abline() functions, what is the height at which the clustering model has 4 clusters?

```{r}
plot(wisc.hclust)
abline(h = 19, col="red", lty=2)

```

At height 19, the clustering model has 4 clusters!

### Selecting Number of Clusters 

Now, we can cut the tree into 4 clusters: 

```{r}
wisc.hclust.clusters <- cutree(wisc.hclust, k = 4)
```

After compare the cluster membership to actual diagnoses: 

```{r}
table(wisc.hclust.clusters, diagnosis)
```

### Using Different Methods 

Run 4 different clustering methods to try and choose my favorite!! 

>Q12. Which method gives your favorite results for the same data.dist dataset? Explain your reasoning.

```{r}
single <- hclust(data.dist, method = "single")
plot(single)

complete <- hclust(data.dist, method = "complete")
plot(complete)

average <- hclust(data.dist, method = "average")
plot(average)

ward.D2 <- hclust(data.dist, method = "ward.D2")
plot(ward.D2)
```

Just like the professor, I also like the Ward.D2 function because it gives my analysis a cleaner look and is easier to understand! Compared to the other methods, this dendogram creates two distrinct branches which helps me understand that data are organized into these two main clusters. By doing this, it minimizes the variations and helps me organize similar observations with each other (which makes it easier for me to analyze patterns when trying to figure out similarities). 

# Combining Methods 

Taking the PCA results I have made, it is time to use it for hierarchical clustering! 

First, create my new clustering model: 

```{r}
wisc.pr.hclust <- hclust(dist(wisc.pr$x[, 1:7]), method = "ward.D2")

plot(wisc.pr.hclust)
```

Time to divide the dendogram into two clusters 

```{r}
grps <- cutree(wisc.pr.hclust, k=2)
table(grps)
```

Comparing clusters with our diaganoses 

```{r}
table(grps, diagnosis)
```

NOW FINALLY....plot the clusters of PC1 vs PC2: 

```{r}
ggplot(wisc.pr$x) +
  aes(PC1, PC2) +
  geom_point(col=grps)
```

Now, construct the hierarchical clustering code and cut into 2 clusters: 

```{r}
wisc.pr.hclust <- hclust(dist(wisc.pr$x[,1:7]), method="ward.D2")

wisc.pr.hclust
```

```{r}
wisc.pr.hclust.clusters <- cutree(wisc.pr.hclust, k=2)
```

>Q13. How well does the newly created hclust model with two clusters separate out the two “M” and “B” diagnoses?

```{r}
table(wisc.pr.hclust.clusters, diagnosis)
```

Based on the code, the new function of hclust separates malignant and benign samples pretty well! In the table above, in C1 it has mainly malignant samples while C2 has benign samples! As a result, showing the distinction between the two diagnoses help conclude that PCA with hierarchical clustering is super useful for discovering patterns! 

>Q14. How well do the hierarchical clustering models you created in the previous sections (i.e. without first doing PCA) do in terms of separating the diagnoses? Again, use the table() function to compare the output of each model (wisc.hclust.clusters and wisc.pr.hclust.clusters) with the vector containing the actual diagnoses.

```{r}
table(wisc.hclust.clusters, diagnosis)
table(wisc.pr.hclust.clusters, diagnosis)
```
Based on the comparison, the model without PCA was a lot more disorganized. It divided it into 4 clusters even if they were split into benign and malignant. However, we only saw actual differences in cluster 1 and 3 where cluster 1 showed more malignant while cluster 3 showed more benign. On the other hand, the model with PCA created only two clusters. Overall, while both provided useful information, the one with PCA is easier to interpret because it only shows the two clusters that are in relation with the diagnoses of malignant and benign!

# Prediction 

Now we will take our PCA model from before and new cancer cell data to observe! 

```{r}
#url <- "new_samples.csv"
url <- "https://tinyurl.com/new-samples-CSV"
new <- read.csv(url)
npc <- predict(wisc.pr, newdata=new)
npc
```

Plot the new data: 

```{r}
plot(wisc.pr$x[,1:2], col=grps)
points(npc[,1], npc[,2], col="blue", pch=16, cex=3)
text(npc[,1], npc[,2], c(1,2), col="white")
```

>Q16. Which of these new patients should we prioritize for follow up based on your results?

Based on the results, we should be prioritizing patient 2 for the follow up!
